title: De insigni paradoxo, quod in analysi maximorum et minimorum occurrit

deep.reconstruction: This first page states the problem and the two paradoxes; the computation begins on p.17. Take a horizontal line AB and measure depth below it by x (x = YV), with horizontal coordinate y. Among curves joining two given points below AB, minimise J = ∫√x ds = ∫√(x(1+p²)) dx, where p = dy/dx. On the next page Euler reads √x as the speed of a body falling from rest at the level of AB, so J is Maupertuis' action, and he concludes that the extremals are free projectile paths. These are parabolas with AB as common directrix. The Euler–Lagrange first integral is √x·p/√(1+p²) = const, which gives parabolas whose directrix is AB. Paradox 1: often a different curve between the same endpoints gives a smaller J than the computed parabola. The natural candidate goes vertically up to AB, runs along AB where the integrand vanishes, and comes back down. Its cost is (2/3)(a^{3/2}+b^{3/2}), with a and b the endpoint depths. For endpoints far enough apart horizontally this beats the parabola. Paradox 2: for some endpoints no real extremal exists; the parabolas from one point with directrix AB fill only the region under their envelope (the 'safety parabola'). Yet J clearly takes larger and smaller values on admissible curves, so a minimum ought to exist. In modern terms: the extremal parabola is only a weak or local minimum, and global optimality fails past the conjugate point (Jacobi's condition). The integrand degenerates on AB, so the true infimum comes from a broken, Goldschmidt-type path along the degenerate boundary. Equivalently, √x ds is the Jacobi–Maupertuis metric for uniform gravity, which degenerates on the zero-velocity line (the boundary of the Hill region).

ideas.what: Variational problem ∫√x ds below a horizontal line (the action of a heavy body falling from rest at that line)
ideas.modern_name: Jacobi–Maupertuis metric for uniform gravity; least action
ideas.usually_credited_to: Maupertuis/Euler (1744); Jacobi (1837/1866) for the metric form
ideas.where_published: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (1744), Additamentum II; E735 itself

ideas.what: Computed extremal is not the true minimum; competing broken curves give a smaller value
ideas.modern_name: Weak vs strong/global minimum; conjugate points (Jacobi condition); Goldschmidt-type discontinuous solution
ideas.where_published: E735 (Mémoires de l'Académie de St.-Pétersbourg III, 1811); discussed by Carathéodory in the Opera omnia introduction to I.25 (unsure of exact pages)

ideas.what: Extremal becomes imaginary for certain endpoints although the functional is bounded below
ideas.modern_name: Nonexistence of an extremal beyond the envelope (safety parabola / caustic); infimum attained only in a relaxed or degenerate sense

missed.claim: Euler's paradox is an early explicit instance of the degeneracy of the Jacobi–Maupertuis metric at the zero-velocity curve (Hill boundary). In that metric, paths that touch or run along the boundary are 'shorter' than the true dynamical orbits, and the orbits stop being minimising beyond the caustic. This links Euler 1779 to modern work on Jacobi-metric geodesics reaching the Hill boundary and on brake orbits (Seifert 1948 onward). Those works do not, to my knowledge, cite Euler.
missed.quote: pluribus casibus aliae lineae exhiberi possunt, pro quibus ista summa minor reperiatur quam in curva per calculum inventa
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historiographical: Euler identified that least action fails as a global principle near the zero-velocity boundary well before Jacobi. This is a precedent for the degenerate-metric phenomena studied in celestial mechanics.

deep.surprise_reason: The paper and its paradox are known. It is discussed in the Opera omnia editorial material and in histories of the calculus of variations as a precursor of the Jacobi and Weierstrass sufficiency theory. This page itself only states the problem; the only modest point is the under-cited link to Jacobi-metric degeneracy at the Hill boundary.
